content.text:
Three separate things got mixed. One at a time.

**1. What the brackets hold, and why `v` is the problem.** In `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` the four names are static parameters of the type, the same kind of thing as the `16` in `Array[\RR64, 16\]`. A static parameter that is a number is a `nat` in Fortress, and a `nat` is an `NN32`, a 32-bit natural. The last parameter, `v`, is the numeral's digits read as one integer. For `3.1415926535897932384` that is a 20-digit integer, which no `NN32` holds. So the Draft's own example cannot be a type argument under the Draft's own `nat`. That is all I meant by "can't be built as written". ("Net" in your dictation is `nat`.)

**2. Where the text is.** The frozen Draft has the numeral family at `literals.tex:83-129`. The revised `Specification/` still has that passage, word for word, and after it the revision box of September at `:149-165`, which says the library gives an integer numeral the type `IntLiteral`. So the revised text today says both: the Draft's family, and the box. The rung that builds P-172 has to make them one passage. That is where I got both names from, and why I kept saying "the Draft's types": they are still in the text, and nobody built them.

**3. The interval, three ways.** A coercion is declared inside the type that receives it; the library's own reads `coerce(x: IntLiteral) = Ratio(x.asZZ, 1)` in `QQ` (`FortressLibrary.fss:563`).

The Draft's way, never built. The coercion is generic over the four numbers, and uses them as values:
```
object Interval(lo: RR64, hi: RR64)
  coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) =
    Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))
end
iv: Interval = 3.1415926535897932384
```
The compiler knows `n, m, r, v` for each numeral, so this could even run at compile time. Besides `v` not fitting a `nat`, the checker would instantiate this coercion once per numeral, and a `nat` used as a value is refused under walk today (row 486).

Today's way, on both paths. It works, but gets a double:
```
object Interval(lo: RR64, hi: RR64)
  coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = Interval(x.asRR64, x.asRR64)
end
```
The exact value is gone before your code runs; walk also offers `x.asString`, the text, which you'd have to parse.

The hybrid's way. The same four numbers, as getters on the literal value instead of parameters of its type:
```
object Interval(lo: RR64, hi: RR64)
  coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = do
    q: QQ = x.exactValue      (* v over r to the power m, in lowest terms *)
    Interval(roundDown(q), roundUp(q))
  end
end
iv: Interval = 3.1415926535897932384
```
`FloatLiteral` would declare getters such as `exactValue`, `radix` and `digitsAfterPoint`; the names are the rung's to pick. The library's own `QQ` would use the same getter in its coercion. This is the Draft's promise with the value moved out of the type, where a `nat` could not hold it, into the value, where a `ZZ` can.

content.text:
You could. Nothing in the JVM stops it: a stamped class name is text, and text holds a 20-digit number as well as a 2-digit one. The reasons not to are elsewhere.

- **`nat` is the sizes' type.** Every array, vector and matrix carries its sizes as `nat` parameters, and those become `NN32` values at run time, matching the JVM's `int` indices. Widening `nat` to `ZZ` would make every size an arbitrary-precision integer, for a feature only numerals need.
- **A type per numeral.** With the value in the type, each distinct numeral is its own instantiation: a class per numeral on the compiled path, a type object per numeral under walk, and `3 + 4` needs the checker to compute `7` at the type level, so the checker gets arbitrary-precision arithmetic over static parameters. All of this to carry a number the checker already has: it reads the digits off the literal node.
- **No gain over getters.** What the Draft wanted is that a conversion sees `n, m, r, v`. A getter on the literal value gives the same four numbers to the same coercion, and the compiler, which knows them at compile time, can still fold the conversion or refuse a range statically by reading the literal node. The type-level version adds only one thing: a coercion could be declared for one specific numeral value. Nobody needs that.
- **The team walked away from it.** They built the two plain types in the prelude instead, between 2009 and 2012.

So it isn't impossible, it's expensive and buys nothing. The getters keep the Draft's promise and leave `nat` alone.

content.text:
The checker can do that today, with no magic: it already holds every numeral's digits, base and point position on the literal node, at any size. Keeping a type `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` with a big `v` inside the checker would be a second copy of the same information. Nothing stops it, and nothing is gained by it. The question is only what reaches run time, and there "compile-time only" splits in two:

- **A built-in target.** `r: RR64 = 3.1415926535897932384`, `q: QQ = 0.1`, `z: ZZ32 = 3`. The compiler knows the digits and the target, so it computes the result and emits the constant. Compile-time only, no literal value anywhere. That is B's fold.
- **A program's own target.** `iv: Interval = 3.1415926535897932384`. The conversion is the body of your `coerce`, ordinary Fortress code that the compiler does not evaluate; it runs at run time, and it needs the digits as values then. So the digits must reach run time somehow, and there are only two ways: as static parameters of a generic coercion, which the compiled path realizes by making a class per instantiation, one per numeral, since Fortress specialises generics like C# and does not erase them like Java; or as fields of one value that the coercion receives, which is a literal value with getters. Haskell does the second: `fromRational` hands the user's type a `Rational` at run time.

So "never at run time" holds for every built-in type, and for a program's own type the literal must appear once at run time, as the argument of its coercion, under any design. The hybrid is just the cheapest form of that: one value with the four numbers on it, no class per numeral, no second type system in the checker.

content.text:
You're right, and I overstated it. Two things to set straight:

- **`nat` on the compiled path is the revival's work.** The checker's handling of `nat` and `int` static parameters came from a revival rung (F-67, which builds your decision P-40), and sizes carried at run time as descriptors from another (F-129, your P-41). The team's interpreter did read `nat` parameters in its library, such as `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, but the team's compiler never finished them. So "the team walked away from the Draft's numeral types because `nat` is 32-bit" is not a claim the record supports, and I shouldn't have put it that way.
- **What the record does support:** the team never declared the Draft's numeral types in any library (F-169), left the note "we need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy" beside them, and built `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` in the prelude instead. Why they chose that, nobody wrote down. The 32-bit `nat` is a limit of the implementation as it stands today, ours included, not a reason the team gave.

The argument against carrying the digits in the type stays what it was in the last two messages: a type per numeral, type-level arithmetic for `3 + 4`, and no gain over the same four numbers as getters on the value. But its source is our reading of the code, not the team's history.

input.message:
One more design to cost by reading only, beside the hybrid, at the curator's question; no build. The Working Draft's own way for a program's type: the numeral's type carries the four numbers as `nat` static parameters, `RadixPointNumeral[
, m, r, v\]` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:110-129`), and a program's type declares a generic coercion over them, `coerce[
at n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[
, m, r, v\])`, whose body uses `n, m, r, v` as values; at an untyped place reading B's default still applies, so these types live only in the checker, except that a coercion instantiated for a numeral is realised the way the compiled path realises every generic, a specialised class per instantiation, with the static arguments stamped in (F-129: a size read as a value is a constant the class loader replaces). Cost, by reading, what each path must change: the checker typing a numeral with four static arguments and inferring a generic coercion's static arguments from them (does the checker accept static parameters on a coercion today? row 513 says walk does not convert through one); `nat` beyond 32 bits in the checker's size arithmetic (F-67, F-146) and in the class loader's stamped constants (F-129), since `v` of a 20-digit numeral exceeds an `NN32`; walk's `nat` used as a value (row 486) and its instantiation per numeral; and whether a `where` clause on such a coercion, `where { v < 256 }`, could refuse an out-of-range numeral at compile time, which the hybrid cannot. Say what this way gains over the hybrid (no run-time literal value even for a program's type; static range checks) and what it costs beyond it, with the same three tests (round trip, decimal, equivalence by value across bases) judged by reading. Keep the four-hour bound; list what you leave.

272	### 7.1 A hybrid
273	
274	**The hybrid.** B's default where nothing fixes a type; but a program's own type may still declare `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` and receives the exact literal, so that a literal value exists at run time only as the argument of such a coercion. This is Haskell's `fromInteger` and `fromRational` for a user's type beside B's (Swift's) default elsewhere; Swift's `ExpressibleByFloatLiteral` hands a `Double` and loses (the coordinator's framing, from their documentation as I know it, not run here).
275	
276	**What it keeps of B's gains.**
277	- No literal value at an untyped place, in a generic, at `SEQV`, or in the library's own number types, whose coercions the fold still makes constants. `Cell(3)` a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, `x SEQV z` true, row 946 gone.
278	- `IntLiteral`'s 19 operator bindings stay deleted. Of the 24, the literal's accessors that a program's coercion reads must stay, with P-169's compiled carrier: `IntLiteral`'s `asZZ` (`ToZZ`; the other conversions are Fortress text over it) and, optionally, `asFloat` (`AsFloat`, which can be Fortress text over `asZZ`); `FloatLiteral`'s 3; and an accessor for the exact value, which none of the 24 gives (below). So 4 or 5 bindings and one or two new getters, against 24 under A and 3 (walk's, until its rung) under B.
279	
280	**The accessors.** The Working Draft's four parameters (`literals.tex:110-129`, `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]`): for a numeral with a radix point, the digit count `n`, the count after the point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v`; for an integer numeral, the radix and the value. As getters, not static parameters:
281	- the one library: `FloatLiteral` declares `getter digits(): ZZ32`, `getter fractionDigits(): ZZ32`, `getter radix(): ZZ32`, `getter digitValue(): ZZ`, and, derived in Fortress, `numerator(self): ZZ` and `denominator(self): ZZ` reduced (`v / r^m`); `IntLiteral` declares `getter radix(): ZZ32` beside `asZZ`. content.text:
Here it is, step by step, with the terms first.

**Terms**
- **Numeral**: the digits written in the program, such as `3.14159` or `C.8_16`.
- **Compile time**: when the compiler reads the program and writes the class files.
- **Load time**: when the JVM loads a class file, once, before the program's code in it runs.
- **Run time**: when the JVM executes the program's code, each time the code is reached.
- **Coercion**: a conversion that the compiler inserts where a value of one type is used where another type is declared. Its body is library or program code.
- **Constant folding**: the compiler computes an expression at compile time and writes the result into the class file in place of the expression.

**What constant folding needs**
1. Every operand of the expression is a constant.
2. The compiler has the rule of the operation inside itself. It does not need to run any code of the program to get the result.
3. The result is a value that a class file can hold as a constant. A JVM class file holds five kinds: `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` and `String`.

**Cases that meet all three**
- `3 + 4`: the operands are numerals, the compiler knows `+` on integers, the result 7 is an `int`.
- `r: RR64 = 3.14159`: the operand is a numeral, the compiler knows how to round a rational to the nearest double, the result is a `double`.
- `q: QQ = 1/2`: the compiler knows rational arithmetic; the result is two integers, 1 and 2, which the class file holds.
- The prototype did these. This is the constant folding the Draft describes for "static expressions".

**The case that does not meet them**: `iv: Interval = 3.14159`, where `Interval` is a type that the program declares with its own `coerce`.
1. The operand is a constant. Met.
2. The operation is the body of the program's `coerce`. The compiler has no rule for it. The body is Fortress code: it can call functions, make objects, loop. To fold it, the compiler would have to execute Fortress code while compiling. No Fortress compiler can do that, the team's or ours. The only program that executes Fortress is walk. Not met.
3. The result is an `Interval` object. A class file cannot hold an object as a constant. Not met.

So this case is not constant folding. It is the same shape, but step 2 fails, and step 3 would fail even if step 2 passed. That is the whole difference: folding works where the compiler knows the operation, and a program's coercion is an operation the compiler does not know.

**What the Draft says.** It promises compile-time computation for static expressions: the quotient of two integer numerals, and a numeral with an exponent, converted to a float with one rounding (`literals.tex:166-173`). Those are built-in operations on numerals. It says that libraries define the coercions from numerals, and it does not say that the compiler executes a coercion's body. So the Draft asks for the folding the prototype did, and not for the folding of a program's coercion.

**The nearest the JVM allows for a program's type.** The compiler writes the numeral's four numbers as constants into the class file, and writes a call of the program's `coerce` with them into the class's initializer. The JVM runs that call once, at load time, and stores the result in a `static final` field. Every later use reads the field. The JIT treats the field as a constant. The body runs once per class, never per use.

**Where this leaves the two designs.** In both, the body gets the four numbers and runs once at load. In the hybrid they arrive as the fields of one argument. In the Draft's way they arrive as four static parameters, stamped into a class of their own per numeral. Same numbers, same single run, different plumbing. The hybrid needs no new kind of type and no class per numeral.

**The one way to get your full picture**, the object computed at compile time: give the compiler an evaluator for Fortress, which means running walk inside the compiler to execute coercion bodies, and then generating code that rebuilds the resulting object's fields at load time, since the file still cannot hold the object. That is compile-time execution of user code, Zig's `comptime`. It is a project of its own, and it would still end in a load-time construction of the object. Nobody has built it for Fortress.

Yes, it reconciles, with one open contradiction and one change of form, both of which Appendix I can carry. Sentence by sentence against the Draft (`literals.tex:25-26`, `:132-148`, `:160-175`):

**Where your design is a plain reading of the text:**
- "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation." Your numeral is four numbers known at compile time. Kept.
- "This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations." This is your design exactly: the type's coercion receives the numeral and decides. The Draft names this as the purpose of numeral types, and your design is the first that delivers it, since neither path hands a program's type the digits today.
- "Libraries define coercions from numerals to integers and rational numbers." Kept; the compiler folds them.
- "Numerals have their own types", with `n, m, r, v`. Kept in content: the numeral carries exactly those four numbers to every conversion.
- "The compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring at most one floating-point rounding error." Kept; that is the fold.
- "In general rational computations may also be performed at run time." Kept; `QQ` stays.

**Where it changes the form, not the content.** The Draft puts `n, m, r, v` into the type as static parameters; your design puts them into the numeral's value as fields, one type per kind of numeral. Same four numbers, same coercion. The team's own prelude made this change first, with `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`, so the revision follows the team's later practice over the Draft's unfinished form.

**Where it contradicts the Draft.** One sentence: "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types because ... we expect them to be polymorphic." Your design keeps that at every place that fixes a type and drops it where none does: there the numeral takes `ZZ32` by size or `RR64`. The Draft would keep the numeral's own type there, and the restart would give it `QQ` or `NN`. This is reading B's one bend, and the revision form records it with its reason: the peers' rule, no literal value at run time, and the digits still reaching every conversion that has a type to convert into. A smaller one beside it: a program may name `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral` only in a coercion's parameter, where the Draft would let a variable carry a numeral type.

So you contradict the Draft in one clause, knowingly, and you fulfil its stated purpose where both implementations and the prelude had left it unfulfilled. That is within the right you reserved, and it is a cleaner revision than most on record.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- Put into a batch record every piece of work on PLAN's road that moves the project forward and is well defined: its decisions are taken. A new deliverable still waits for its go (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"). A piece that is not well defined waits. A well-defined piece waits only if it would put the batch's merge at risk. Two rungs put it at risk if the gather cannot merge their edits of one file or one declaration cleanly. A pair that merges cleanly but changes one behaviour two ways, or where one needs the other's result, goes in one batch only if one lands only with the other (the manifest's `landsOnlyWith`).
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

The scout found the team's words, and they don't say what we expected. I have to tell you before the writer records a reason the sources contradict.

**What the team said about `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`:**
- Jan-Willem Maessen, 17 November 2009, the commit that made `IntLiteral` a type apart from `ZZ32`: "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec. Over the next few weeks expect more coercions to come on line as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric hierarchy." A joint effort with the Austin group, "and now it actually works!"
- David Chase, 31 August 2009: "ZZ32 is NOT a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64; this would be a good time to get coercion working."
- The only `HACK` and `TODO` lines are walk's: `FFloatLiteral`'s equivalence, "HACK that's only sort-of correct. If we care about all the digits, there must be some sort of normalization" (Maessen, 2008), and "literals don't support asString due to dotted method inheritance bugs" (2009).
- No team comment, note or commit calls the two types temporary, a stopgap, or the final design. No team code names `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`. The record's own quote, "do not enable these until coercion is implemented", is Maessen's of July 2008, about walk's library, and says the arithmetic waited for coercion, not that the type was a stopgap.

**What that means for the entry.** The team saw `IntLiteral` as building the spec's coercion of numerals, and they built it alike for all the number types. Under your own P-26 that counts as their later word, so "the team's temporary hack" is a reason the sources don't bear out, and the writer must not put it in POSITIONS.

A reason the sources do bear out: the team built the Draft's coercion of numerals under names of their own, with the exact value in the numeral, and never the rest of the Draft's design, the four numbers that a program's type can read. Your decision keeps what they built, one type per kind of numeral with the exact value at the coercion, and completes it with the Draft's names and the Draft's four numbers. That is a revision of the team's later word in two places, the names and the fields, taken by your right to finish the specification, and Appendix I says so.

Does the decision stand with that reason? If yes, the writer runs now.

**1. The numeral types themselves,** `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`: each numeral "has type `NaturalNumeral[\n, 10, v\]`", "has type `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, 10, v\]`", and "every numeral also has type `Numeral[\n, m, r, v\]`". Between them, the team's own note: "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy. All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given." No example of a variable declared with a numeral type is anywhere in the Draft. My "as the Draft allows" rested only on the general rule that any type can be a variable's type. Withdraw it; the Draft never shows that use.

**2. Where the Draft uses the numeral types,** and the only place: the chapter on binary words, `advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1661`, a library the team never built (its text says "Description to be supplied"). There a word of bits takes a numeral by a coercion:
```
coerce[\nat m, nat radix, nat q, nat k, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\m, radix, v\])
  where { radix = 2^q, q DOT m = n DOT 2^b }
```
and concatenates with one: `opr ||(self, other: NaturalNumeral[\m, radix, v\])`. Read it: `radix = 2^q` says the numeral must be written in base 2, 4, 8 or 16; `q DOT m = n DOT 2^b` says the digit count times the bits per digit must equal the word's width. So `FF_16` is a word of 8 bits, `1010_2` a word of 4 bits, and `255` is refused, because base 10 is no power of two. The digit count and the base carry meaning here that neither a `ZZ` nor a double has. This is the Draft's one worked example of your design, and the best stress test we have.

**3. Do they work as written?** No, and not only for the names:
- The static-expression machinery they rest on was never built: `constant.tex:14` opens "Static expressions are not yet supported", and the constant types it describes, such as `IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]`, exist nowhere.
- With the four numbers as fields, as you decided, the coercion works and its `where` conditions become run-time checks in the coercion's body: fine. But the word's width in the example is a static parameter derived from the numeral's digits, `n` from `q DOT m`. A field cannot feed a static parameter. So `w = FF_16` could not be typed as an 8-bit word at compile time; the type would have to be written, `w: BinaryWord[\8\] = FF_16`, and the coercion would check the digit count against 8 at load. That is the one thing the Draft's static-parameter form can do and the field form cannot: let a numeral's shape pick a type's size. Nothing in the library needs it today.

**4. The finer point.** Under B no numeral value lives on in the program. A numeral exists for one moment, as the argument of a coercion or an operator that declares a numeral type as its parameter, as the binary chapter does, and then it has become the target type. If a program could write `x: RadixPointNumeral = 0.5`, the numeral would live in `x`, and we would be back to a literal value at run time. So the sub-choice: a numeral type may be written as a parameter type, in a coercion or an operator, exactly as the Draft uses it, and not as a variable's, field's or return type. That default matches the Draft's own use and adds the restriction only where the Draft shows nothing.

input.prompt:
You are the judge of one design question in the Fortress revival, /home/user/fortress. Load the `fortress-repo` skill (/home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md) and read its `references/revival-changes.md` and `references/specification.md`. The curator (the person in charge) has decided a design for numerals, the numeric literals of a program, and asks you to judge whether it is internally coherent, where it bends the specification, and what test cases pin it, before it is written into the record and planned as a batch. You judge; you write a judgement file; you change nothing else and commit nothing.

## The decision, in the curator's words and the coordinator's condensation (2026-11-08)

1. Where no type is declared, a numeral takes the machine default: an integer numeral becomes `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and a numeral with a radix point becomes `RR64`. "We'll go with machine defaults. When the type is not declared." The places that fix no type: an untyped binding `x = 3`, a parameter of type `Any`, a static argument that only the numeral fixes (`Cell(3)`, `<|1, 2, 3|>`), the operands of `SEQV` or `=` with no typed side, a tie between two coercions (a float numeral tied between `QQ` and `RR64` reads `RR64`).
2. Where a type is fixed, the compiler converts the numeral at compile time from its exact value: exactly into the integer types and `QQ`, with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (the Working Draft's "at most one floating-point rounding error"). Walk converts from the exact value at the same places.
3. The numeral types are the Working Draft's: `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, carrying the Draft's four numbers as fields of the numeral's value, not as static parameters of its type: the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`). The implementations' names `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` go.
4. A program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from the numeral type, written `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)` inside the type, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits that call once per class, at load, with the numbers as constants. "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." No numeral value lives on past such a call.
5. Sub-choices, taken as defaults for the curator's review: the library's `=` pairs over the numeral types stay and fold into constants; `gg(5, w)` with `gg` overloaded at `(ZZ32, T)` and `(Any, Any)` takes the `ZZ32` declaration; `x = 7/2` stays a `QQ` and a comparison of literals alone folds, so `1/2 = 0.5` is true; a numeral type may be written only as a parameter type, in a coercion or an operator, not as a variable's, field's or return type; an expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker; string literals of one text are one object and `"a" || "b"` folds (P-171).
6. The curator's reason: finishing the specification's design for numerals. He weighed and declined the 2012 restart's exact defaults (`ZZ`, `QQ`), because microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would become rationals and need typed lines, and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`.

## The sources, which you read

- The Working Draft: `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:25-26`, `:83-129`, `:132-175`; `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/constant.tex:13-60` (static expressions, "not yet supported"); the one use of the numeral types, `Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1596-1661`, a coercion and an `opr ||` over `NaturalNumeral[\m, radix, v\]` with `where` clauses that derive a binary word's width from the digit count and the radix; `basic/conversions-coercions.tex:98-101`; `basic/variables.tex:75`.
- The revised text today: `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:149-165`, the revival's box that names `IntLiteral`.
- The 2012 restart: `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/Expressions/literals.tick:25`, `types.tick:970-980`.
- The record, through `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `P-26`, `P-74`, `P-76`, `P-165`, `P-168`, `P-171`, `P-172`, `P-40`, `P-41`, `F-169`, `F-57`, `F-73`, and `history:P-76`.
- The reviews: `explorations/reviews/literals-2026-11-08.md` (sections 1.1, 2, 6), `explorations/reviews/literals-one-picture-2026-11-08.md`, `explorations/reviews/literal-fork-2026-11-08.md` (sections 2, 3.6, 4, 5, 6, 7), and the prototype's report `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md` (sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11), whose patch built points 1, 2 and 5 on the compiled side, with `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` as the names.
- The team's words on the two names: `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/numeral-names/evidence.md` (a scout's file; the team called the two neither temporary nor final; Maessen's commit of 2009-11-17: "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec").

## What you judge

1. **Coherence.** Is the design one rule with one answer for every case? List any case where two of its points give two answers, or where a point is undefined (for example: a numeral at a parameter of type `Number`; a numeral in a tuple at `Any`; a numeral in an `if` join; `-3` as prefix minus on a `NaturalNumeral`; `x = 3` then `x` at a `ZZ64` place, where `x` is a `ZZ32`; a `nat` parameter used as a value; `pi: RadixPointNumeral` in the library's `Constants.fsi`; what `SEQV` answers between two numeral values inside a coercion's body).
2. **Against the record.** Which decisions on record it revises (expected: P-76, P-172, and P-172's clause on places that fix no type), and whether it contradicts any other, with the entry's words.
3. **Against the Draft.** Each sentence of the Draft it keeps as written, each it changes in form only (the four numbers as fields), and each it contradicts (expected: numerals "not directly converted ... polymorphic" at places that fix no type; the binary chapter's static width from the digit count, which fields cannot feed). Say for the binary example what the design can and cannot give it.
4. **The sub-choices.** For each default of point 5, say whether it follows from points 1 to 4, is a free choice, or conflicts with them; where it is free, say which way the Draft, the library's way (P-74, P-165) and the peers point.
5. **The test cases.** List the programs that pin the design on both paths, each with its expected answer under the design and its answer today, grouped: the defaults (`x = 3`, `y = 0.5`, `Cell(3)`, `<|1,2,3|>`, `f(3)` at `Any`, `3 SEQV z`, `1/2 = 0.5`, `x = 7/2`, `1 - b` for `b = 0.9`, `1.0 s`); the typed places (`q: QQ = 0.1`, `r: RR64 = 0.1`, `z: ZZ32 = 3000000000` refused, a 17-digit numeral rounded once, `n: NN32 = 5`); a program's own type (a complex `CC64` from `3 + 4 i` and `3.78 + 3.243 i`; an interval enclosing `0.1`; a bfloat16 rounding once where a double rounds twice, the prototype's `1.00390625000000000001`; a decimal `Dec(314159, 5)` from `3.14159`; a round trip that prints `C.8_16` back as written); equivalence by value (`0.1_2 SEQV 0.5` true, `0.1 = 0.1_16` false, `2.5 SEQV 2.50` true, `"" 2.50` printing); strings (`"ab" SEQV "ab"`, `("a" || "b") SEQV "ab"`); and microGPT's lines (`MicroGptFlat.fss:17-18`, `:77-79`, `:82`, `:59`, `:66`; `MicroGptApl.fss:26-27`, `:106`, `:112`), with the tie rule. Mark each case the prototype already measured.
6. **What stays open** for the curator, as decisions not taken, in one line each.

## Form

Write `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/literal-judgement/JUDGEMENT.md` (create the folder; if writing is refused, return the whole text as your final message). Markdown, lists not tables, plain short sentences, every claim with its source (file:line, entry number, review section). Name the curator "the curator" and the coordinating session "the coordinator". Main text at most 9K characters; an appendix may add citations. End with a summary under 300 words that gives your verdict in one sentence first: coherent as stated, coherent with the changes you name, or not coherent. Final message under 300 words: the file's path and the verdict with the changes, if any.

The condition `q DOT m = n DOT 2^b` says "digits times bits per digit equals words times bits per word". It is arithmetic on static parameters that the checker would have to solve, the static-expression system the Draft marks "not yet supported". We won't fulfil that chapter, and your coercion is a different mechanism: a call with the four numbers as values. The design is yours, and I'll record it as such.

content.text:
You're not mixing things up. Natural numbers are the non-negative ones, and the Draft's numerals are exactly that: a numeral is digits, a radix point and a radix specifier, never a sign. `-3` is not a numeral; it is the prefix operator `-` applied to the numeral `3`. So `NaturalNumeral` is the right name for what the parser hands over, and the sign lives in the expression around it.

What that means under the design:
- At a typed place, `z: ZZ32 = -3` is `-(3)` with `3` converted first. The compiled path already folds this: a prefix minus on a numeral becomes a negative constant before the checker (F-262 records that a numeral's sign does not reach its type).
- With the fold of expressions of literals alone, `-3`, `3 + 4` and `1/2` become one exact signed value before anything else, and that value converts or defaults like a numeral. One trap this avoids: `-2147483648`, the smallest `ZZ32`. Read as `-(2147483648)` with the default first, the inner numeral doesn't fit `ZZ32`, becomes a `ZZ64`, and the result is a `ZZ64`; Java has a special grammar rule for this one literal. Folding first gives the exact value, which fits `ZZ32`.
- For a program's own type, `c: CC64 = -3` is `-(3)`: the coercion receives the numeral `3` with its four numbers, and the type's own prefix `-` applies to the result. A type that cannot be negated refuses it, as it should.

I put `-3` among the cases the judge checks, so its report says whether the design states this order, fold first, then convert or default, or leaves it to be said.

- The gather is reductions and products, including the embedding gradients, written as one-hot products (`MicroGptFlat.fss:70`; APL `MicroGptApl.fss:96`). **No transaction is ever opened.**

**On the compiled path, with unboxed arrays and views** (P-17, P-84, F-11, F-12, F-40, F-301):
- **The pool and `do … also`.** Loops over views fork per arm. This is sound with disjoint writes (§5), but the one library splits to single elements with no grain size (`RangeInternals.fss:1324-1340`). Each split builds a task object even when it is not forked (`CodeGen.java:1667-1689`).
- **Reductions.** They will run in sequence (N5). Every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of the model loses its parallelism unless the code generator or the library changes.
- **Abrupt completion.** Any exception in a forked arm, such as `IntegerOverflow`, an index fault in a view, or an `assert`, leaves sibling arms writing arrays after the caller has moved on (N1).
- **The per-access transaction check.** It stays on mutable locals (row 641, F-12). For elements, the `Object[]` store checks the thread and the current transaction on every `get` and `put` (`FortressArrayStore.java:35-37`). Whether the unboxed store pays the same is undecided (§8, D1).
- **The STM** is not reached, if the model keeps its shape.

**The gather can be done by reductions alone, as the language intends.** Only a scatter-add, such as an embedding gradient indexed by token, would tempt `atomic`. Both programs avoid it with one-hot products. The library's own authors also chose sequence over atomic increments (`FortressLibrary.fss:3046`, `:3175-3177`). Parallelising the contraction axis needs a reduction, private partial results joined, not `atomic`. Given the cost in §3.3, an atomic gather would be slower than a sequential one.

### 1.8 Library: ranges, generators, reductions, `parloop`

- **The one library's parallel range.** `loop` splits at a power-of-two boundary into `do … also do … end`, down to single elements, with no grain size. `generate` joins the halves as a call's arguments, `red.join(loop'(lo,mid-1), loop'(mid,hi))` (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1308-1342`, `:1320`). The split depends only on `(lo, hi)`, so the join tree is deterministic (`c4-parallelism.md` §4).
- **`GeneratorLibrary.fss`** only composes generators; it has no `also` of its own.
- **Reductions** carry their algebra as objects: `join` and `empty`, with associativity assumed and checked nowhere (`FortressLibrary.fss:3412`; `c4-parallelism.md` §4).
- **`Matrix.mul`** splits rows and columns with `also` and runs the contraction axis in sequence, with the team's comment "If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition" (`FortressLibrary.fss:3046`). A second comment says the cache-oblivious product was dropped "due to lack of support for atomic increment of matrix elements" (`:3175-3177`). That text dates to 2008 at least (moved by jmaessen's library reorganization 1d2680d4d, 2008-03-24).
- **The compiler prelude.** `parloop` halves at the midpoint while the chunk is above `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK`, default 1 (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:357-369`). `gen` passes its halves as call arguments, and `seqgen` binds them as statements (`:381-414`). On the compiled path the two run alike (N5).

**Contention and abort policy, side by side**

| | walk | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| detection | eager: at the conflicting read or write, through visible readers | lazy: at validation, by value, when the global lock has moved |
| who wins | `GreedyManager`: always aborts the other | the first to commit |

- **The one library's parallel range.** `loop` splits at a power-of-two boundary into `do … also do … end`, down to single elements, with no grain size. `generate` joins the halves as a call's arguments, `red.join(loop'(lo,mid-1), loop'(mid,hi))` (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1308-1342`, `:1320`). No prototype exists for the parallelism repairs. The parallelism review measured the defects with probe programs, three runs each at four threads; nothing was built. Today's prototype was the literals. Here is ask 4, from a fresh read of the review's sections 1.8, 6, 7 and 8.

**Ask 4: should the compiled path run a reduction's halves in parallel, and when?**

Primer:
- A reduction is `SUM`, `DOT` or `BIG MAX` over a range or an array. The library splits the range into two halves, computes each, and joins the two results: `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))` (`RangeInternals.fss:1320`). Both halves are the arguments of one call to `join`.
- Under walk the arguments of a call run in parallel, so each half forks and the reduction is a tree of tasks. On the compiled path the code generator evaluates a call's arguments one after another, under the team's own comment "Why isn't this parallel???" (`CodeGen.java:6935-6955`). Measured: 64 slow bodies in a `SUM` run at most one at a time, where a parallel `for` runs four. This is the defect the review calls N5.
- After the switch-over this hits microGPT directly: its whole gather is reductions, `SUM`, `DOT`, `BIG MAX` and the one-hot products, so every one of them would run in sequence on the compiled path. microGPT fast, phase 6, needs this fixed.
- The specification allows either: a call's arguments "may" be evaluated in parallel (`parallelism.tex:89-90`). The language's design, Steele's talks and walk, is parallel by default.
- Beside it, N1, a plain defect with no fork: a `do … also … end` group whose first arm throws does not wait for its other arms, so after the `catch` the other arms are still writing (`CodeGen.java:1662-1712`). Walk joins every arm. The fix is one code-generator rung: join all arms before the group completes abruptly. It is the first repair in the review's order, since an `IntegerOverflow` or an index fault in parallel numeric code otherwise leaves writers running. I'll put it in the batch after this one as a default; it needs no answer.

Options for N5:
1. **The code generator forks a call's arguments**, as it already forks the elements of a tuple, with `ParallelismAnalyzer` deciding which arguments are worth a task. This makes both paths evaluate arguments alike and fixes every reduction and every parallel call at once. One code-generator rung, plus a grain size in the one library's range split, which today splits down to single elements. Cost to watch: a task per argument where the analyzer doesn't prune.
2. **The one library's `generate` binds its two halves as a tuple**, which the code generator already forks. About one line in `RangeInternals.fss`, plus the grain size. Only reductions gain; other calls stay sequential on the compiled path, so walk and the compiled path keep differing on when arguments run in parallel.
3. **Leave reductions sequential** until PLAN's compiled-parallelism step in phase 6. Nothing now; microGPT's first compiled timing is sequential.

How they weigh:
- 1 is the language's rule and the team's stated wish, and it closes a difference between the paths. It is the widest change and needs the analyzer to keep overhead down.
- 2 is cheap and exact for microGPT's need, but it fixes the symptom and leaves the paths apart.
- 3 defers the question to the moment it bites.
- None of them can be tested compiled before the switch-over, since compiled programs run on the prelude until then. So the rung lands in the first batch after the switch-over, whichever you pick; the choice now only sets PLAN's order.

The review: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md, sections 1.8, 6, 7.1 and 8.

My recommendation: 1, with the grain size, in the first batch after the switch-over, with N1 in the batch before it.

Verdict: **coherent with six repairs.** As stated, four cases get two answers and two are undefined. Each repair is a sentence the entry needs, not a change of your decision; I give my default for each.

1. **What "fixes a type".** A declared type that has a coercion from the numeral type, the eight number types and a program's own types, or a numeral type itself. `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded `T`, and no type at all take the default. So `f(3)` at `Number` is a `ZZ32`.
2. **The default applies to a numeral,** a literal after the fold, never to an expression that merely has a numeral type: a variable inside a coercion's body, or a `nat` parameter used as a value, which gets one fixed type. Row 946 was this error. Default for a `nat` as a value: `ZZ32`, your P-40.
3. **The fold yields a signed constant,** as the Draft's constant types carry a sign: an integer result defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient as `QQ`, a result with a radix point as `RR64`. This is what makes `x = 7/2` a `QQ` and `-2147483648` a `ZZ32`; the prototype's fold made `7/2` an `RR64`, against your sub-choice. A program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only.
4. **Several numerals fixing one type parameter,** `<|3000000000, 0.5|>`, an `if` join: the narrowest default that holds every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each converting exactly. Without it the list is refused.
5. **A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type.** The Draft says coercions don't chain; the prototype chained default and own coercion. Default: refuse, so that a type that wants numerals declares the coercion.
6. **"Once per class, at load" as a rule:** a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does under P-171, so two evaluations of `c: CC64 = 3` are one object and `SEQV` sees it.

## The decisions to record, both the curator's, 2026-11-08

Read first, in this order: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, section "Held in chat (2026-11-08)", the lines of 22:3x, 23:3x, 14:2x, 15:0x, 12:4x and 12:1x (his words and the coordinator's condensation); `explorations/reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md` whole (the Fable judgement: six repairs, the sub-choices, the test cases, its section 6); `explorations/reviews/literal-fork-2026-11-08.md` sections 2, 3.6, 5.3, 6, 7; `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md` sections 4.4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11; `explorations/reviews/literals-one-picture-2026-11-08.md`; the scout's evidence on the team's words, `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/numeral-names/evidence.md` (sections 1.2, 3.4, 3.5, 6, 10); and the record: `facts-extract.sh 'P-76+'`, `'history:P-76'`, `'P-172+'`, `'history:P-172'`, `'P-26'`, `'P-74'`, `'P-165'`, `'P-168'`, `'P-169'`, `'P-171'`, `'P-40'`, `'P-49'`, `'F-169'`, `'F-73'`, `'F-74'`, `'F-57'`, `'F-79'`, `'F-262'`, `'P-29'`, and PLAN's phase 4 and phase 6 lines (`grep -n` in `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md` for "String literals, answered", "Float numerals, answered", "parallelism", "N1", "N5").

**Decision 1, the numerals** (his words of 22:3x and 23:3x, the judgement's six repairs accepted, the coordinator's defaults for its open items accepted at 23:3x, "Yeah. Option one."):
1. Where no type is declared, a numeral takes the machine default: an integer numeral `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit; a numeral with a radix point `RR64`. "We'll go with machine defaults. When the type is not declared." A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type (the eight number types, and a program's own type that declares one) or is a numeral type; `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no type take the default. The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression that has a numeral type (row 946 is that error); a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting exactly. A float numeral tied between `QQ` and `RR64` reads `RR64`.
2. Where a type is fixed, the compiler converts the numeral at compile time from its exact value: exactly into the integer types and `QQ`, with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`; an out-of-range numeral is refused statically. Walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker.
3. The numeral types are the Working Draft's (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`): `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` below `Numeral`, carrying the Draft's four numbers as fields of the numeral's value, not as static parameters of its type: the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v`; the explicit-radix variants and `Literal[\v\]` fold into the radix field. The implementations' names `IntLiteral` (the compiler's library, the interpreter's library, P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172) go. A numeral type may be written only as a parameter type, in a coercion or an operator, never as a variable's, field's or return type; the library's `pi: FloatLiteral` becomes `RR64`.
4. A program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from the numeral type, `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)` written inside the type, which reads the four numbers; the compiler emits that call once per class, at load, with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171). "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral. Two numeral values inside a coercion's body compare by their reduced value.
5. An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant: an integer result defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient as `QQ` (so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ` and `1/2 = 0.5` is true through `QQ`'s `=` pair), a result with a radix point as `RR64`; `-3` is prefix minus on the numeral `3`, folded, so `-2147483648` is a `ZZ32`. The library's `=` pairs over the numeral types stay, their conversion folded. `gg(5, w)` with `gg` at `(ZZ32, T)` and `(Any, Any)` takes the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). The binary chapter's `opr ||` with a numeral is dropped.
6. His reason, as the record can bear it: the Working Draft's design for numerals, whose purpose the Draft states ("allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations", `:141-145`), completed. The team built the Draft's coercion of numerals under their own names, with the exact value in the numeral: Jan-Willem Maessen, 2009-11-17, "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec" (the scout's section 1.2); they never built the four numbers that a program's type can read, and no team word calls the two names temporary or final (the scout's section 10). The decision keeps what they built, one type per kind of numeral with the exact value at the coercion, and completes it with the Draft's names and the Draft's four numbers. It bends P-26 in two places, the names and the untyped places, where the prelude's built behaviour, the numeral's own type at every untyped place, is the team's later word; the curator takes that bend by his right to finish the specification, and declined the restart's exact defaults (`ZZ`, `QQ`; `literals.tick:25`) because microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would become rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The one team word for point 4: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). The entry owns this weighing as his, in the record's register, and his dictated words go to the history with their times (08:03, 12:36, 22:3x, 23:3x; the held list has them).
7. What it contradicts in the Draft, for Appendix I at the rung: "not directly converted ... polymorphic" (`:132-141`) at places that fix no type; the binary chapter's static width from the digit count, which fields cannot feed (`binary.tex:1601-1602`, `:1637-1640`). What it keeps and what it changes in form: the judgement's section 3.

Write it as one new POSITIONS entry in Numbers (or split it if `record.md`'s checks ask; keep one owner), reword P-76 and P-172 in place to the new names and the new rule where they state the old (P-76's walk half; P-172's clause "Where nothing fixes a type ... stays an exact FloatLiteral" and "prints a bare numeral as written", a team test, `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16`, that now changes), P-165's name, P-169's 24 numeral bindings (they fall away; the carrier is not designed), with pointers between them. FACTS state the present; change a FACTS entry only where it states a decision now revised (F-169's `IntLiteral` sentence, F-73's tie reading as a default) and leave the measured facts (F-57, F-74, F-79, F-262) for the landing that changes the tree.

**Decision 2, parallel reductions, D3** (his words of 23:3x, "Option one", to the coordinator's ask of 23:1x on `explorations/reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1.8, 6, 7.1 N1 and N5, 8): on the compiled path the code generator evaluates a call's arguments in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as it already forks a tuple's elements and as walk forks arguments, so a reduction's two halves (`red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1320`) run in parallel; the one library's parallel range splits to a grain size, not to single elements. His remark on the grain size, for the history and the entry's why: the split must stop at an efficient chunk, as Steele acknowledges sequential runs at the leaves of the tree in one of his talks, and as Clojure's persistent vectors take a branching factor from B-trees: "you need the right forking constants". N1 (the review's drafted row: a `do … also` group whose first arm completes abruptly does not join its other arms) is a defect with no fork, fixed in the batch before; both land in the first batch after the switch-over, since no compiled program runs the one library before it. Options 2 (the library binds the halves as a tuple) and 3 (leave sequential) declined. One POSITIONS entry, in the section where P-29 and the parallelism decisions sit; a PLAN line for the first batch after the switch-over.

## PLAN

# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
