1	<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
8	- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
9	- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
10	- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
11	- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
12	- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).
13	
14	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15	
16	- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
17	- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.
18	
19	## Decisions on record
20	
21	### The standard and the sources
22	
23	- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
24	- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
25	- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
26	- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
27	- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
28	- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
29	- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
30	- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3 ends when the compiled checker reports no error on the apis and components of the interpreter's library that the distance to the switch-over counts (F-53 defines the distance, says what it counts and holds its value). The library's other components are not part of phase 3: each is cleared before the first program that needs it, and at the latest before walk runs the checker (P-12), so `System` by the switch-over, since the compiler's tests need it (F-293); F-290 counts their errors. Phase 4, the switch-over: first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.
31	- P-175 **On the compiled path a call's arguments run in parallel where `ParallelismAnalyzer` judges them worth a task, as a tuple's elements do, so a reduction's two halves run in parallel; the one library's parallel range stops its split at a grain size, not at single elements.** The one library's range joins a reduction's halves as the arguments of one call, `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))`, and splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1308-1342`); the code generator evaluates a call's arguments in order (F-19, row 951), under the team's comment "Why isn't this parallel???" (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6939`), so every `SUM`, `DOT` and `BIG MAX` of microGPT would run its bodies one at a time once compiled programs run the one library. The split stops at a chunk that runs efficiently in sequence: in his words, "you need the right forking constants", as Steele's parallel trees end in sequential leaves and Clojure's persistent vectors take their branching factor from B-trees. It needs a group of forked arms to join every arm before it completes abruptly, which the compiled path does not do (`CodeGen.genParallelExprs` joins on the normal path only, row 947; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 7.1). The library binding the halves as a tuple, and reductions left in sequence, are declined. Why: the specification evaluates each argument of a call in an implicit thread of its own (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex:60-64`), walk forks a call's arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:342`), and the model's parallelism is its reductions (the review, section 6). Detail: the review, sections 1.8, 6, 7.1 and 8.
32	
33	### The one library and the compiled checker
34	
35	- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.
36	- P-38 **The compiler prelude's own text is not repaired: its defects go with it at the switch-over.** A helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is fixed for the one library, and the prelude's value moves with it (F-313). Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
37	- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. Until the switch-over lands, every batch's gate also measures the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component (F-53), so a native binding moved onto a helper in another component is checked by the distance alone, and P-58 has each moved binding checked from the step that moves it.
38	- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
39	- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
40	- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`.
41	- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
42	- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`. The `where` form is built (P-151), but neither path takes this clause yet: the front end of both paths refuses it on a trait that declares a coercion (row 831), and walk refuses the library at load with it (row 804). `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25), and by them the clause is right as written. The rule leaves a hole that every way of closing `AnyIntegral` shares, except the team's 2008 way, a `comprises` clause on `Integral[\I\]` itself: a program's own subtype of `Integral`, declared in another component, is accepted although no listed type is above it. Row 487 records the hole, and this decision does not close it.
43	- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on three kinds of pair (rows 786 to 788).
44	- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds.
45	- P-47 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, instead of relying on those that it inherits from the generic order traits.** The integer types are the five that `AnyIntegral` lists: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`. Through `Integral`, each inherits the three operators from `StandardTotalOrder` and the `StandardMin`, `StandardMax` and `StandardMinMax` that it extends. `a MINMAX b` is the pair `(a MIN b, a MAX b)`. The `MAX` that a `ZZ64` inherits types `self` as the order trait, so neither it nor `QQ`'s `MAX` is more specific. Under walk, `b MAX 1` for a `ZZ64` `b` would then stop the run with "Ambiguous coercion". With their own declarations, these operators answer at the type that their arguments promote to (P-74), as `b + 1` does. Why: it is the library's own device. `QQ`, `RR64` and the compiler's prelude declare all three, and the specification's `ZZ` declares its own `MIN` and `MAX`.
46	- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding. The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.
47	- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches.
48	- P-50 **The body of a `label` expression, and each value that an `exit` gives it, take the expected type of the whole `label`.** A `label` is a named block that code inside it can leave early with `exit`, giving a value with `with`. The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and the values that its `exit` expressions give. So when a `label` has an expected type, the compiled checker passes it into the body and into each of those values, as it does into each clause of a `typecase`. The specification's inference chapter lists the body and those values as contexts that carry an expected type. P-51 decides the same question for a call written as another call's argument. F-87 lists the checker's contexts that carry an expected type.
49	- P-51 **The checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each declaration's parameter type.** Take an outer call `f(g(x))`, whose argument is an inner call `g(x)`. If none of the compiled checker's attempts at the call accepts `f(g(x))` (P-49 gives the order of those attempts), the checker checks `g(x)` again, once for each declaration of `f`, with that declaration's parameter type at `g(x)`'s position as its expected type. The retry covers every inner call with inferred static arguments, not only one whose type parameter occurs in its result type alone. Why: the curator wants the type inference rules unified across contexts, which covers cases that the team did not build. As built, a generic declaration of `f` is first instantiated from the other arguments. The declaration whose retry succeeds is kept, or the most specific of several; otherwise the call goes on as it would without the retry. The measurement behind the decision is in `explorations/reviews/argument-context-probe.md`.
50	- P-52 **`narrowToRange` on a range of rank 2 or 3 checks containment corner by corner.** `r.narrowToRange(other)` must raise `IndexOutOfBounds` when `other` reaches outside `r` on any axis. Its bounds check compares the two ranges' lower corners, and their upper corners, by `PCMP`, the ranges' own point order, which compares each axis on its own. It does not use the tuples' lexicographic order, which serves sorting. So `((0,0):(9,9)).narrowToRange((2,-1):(5,5))` raises `IndexOutOfBounds`, since -1 lies below 0 on the second axis.
51	- P-53 **`String`'s `left` and `right` answer `Just(c)`, as their declared result type `Maybe[\Char\]` promises.** For a non-empty string, `left` answers `Just` of its first character, and `right` `Just` of its last; for an empty string both answer `Nothing`. The `left` and `right` of the library's ranges and lists answer `Maybe` values in the same way. So walk prints `Just(a)` for `"abc".left`, not `a`.
52	- P-54 **`QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` keep `ZZ`, their declared result type, and raise an error at +∞, −∞ and 0/0.** The specification's paragraph on these methods said that they return the argument itself at those three values (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, "Rational Numbers"). That paragraph is revised. `floor`, `round` and the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉ are built on `ceiling` and `truncate`, so they raise too. Why: the declared integer result and other languages win over the paragraph: Python's `math.floor(inf)`, for one, raises. The library raises `DivisionByZero`, as the revised paragraph says. After the switch-over, `QQ` follows the float ruling (P-68, on rounding the float types): `floor` and `ceiling` return `QQ` and pass the infinities through, and the brackets, `round` and `truncate` give `ZZ` (row 795).
53	- P-55 **A size may hold arithmetic, compared by its written form once its numerals are computed.** The compiled checker accepts a sum, a difference, a product or a power as a size, such as the length in `Vector[\RR64, 16\]`. It computes each operation whose operands are both numerals, from the inside out, so `2 3` is the size `6`. Otherwise it compares two sizes by their written form: `s0 s1` is not the same size as `s1 s0`, though their values are equal. On the compiled path, the class loader computes a size's value when it makes the class of an instantiation. Walk already computes such a size exactly when it makes an instance. The checker counts a size name, such as `b0`, as possibly equal to a numeral, as the team's Q&A in `Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex` answers. So the `N[\0\]` arm of a `typecase N[\b0\]` is reachable. The library keeps the team's sizes written as products and sums, such as a matrix's storage of `s0 s1` cells. F-146 states what the checker accepts.
54	- P-56 **The open range `(:)` keeps its wildcard type, and its five cutting methods fail.** `(:)` is the range of every index, as in `a[:]`. It is the object `TrivialOpenRange`, which stays an `OpenRange[\Any\]`: the team used `Any` as a wildcard for any index type. Its methods `truncL`, `truncR`, `every`, `imposeStride` and `atMost` cut a range, so each must answer a range over `Any`. The library's range operators build ranges only over `ZZ32` and its pairs and triples, and a range over `ZZ32` is not a range over `Any`. So no body that answers a range passes the compiled checker. Each of the five is a `fail` with a message, the team's own device for a body that cannot answer its declared type. Nothing in the tree calls them on `(:)` but the five tests `ProjectFortress/tests/TrivialOpenRange*Stop.fss`, which pin the `fail`. The other way, `(:)` as a range over `ZZ32`, is not taken. Why: a probe under walk tried that way on small programs. More of them stopped with an error where they had printed a result than printed a result where they had stopped (`reviews/ranges-and-index-types.md`, section 5).
55	- P-57 **`LexicographicReduction.isLeftZero` takes `TotalComparison`, so the team's answers are reached.** `LexicographicReduction` is the library's reduction behind `BIG LEXICO`, which combines comparisons in dictionary order. `isLeftZero(c)` says whether `c LEXICO x` is `c` for every `x`. The team declared `isLeftZero(_:EqualTo)` as `false` and `isLeftZero(_:Comparison)` as `true`. `TotalComparison`, whose values are `LessThan`, `EqualTo` and `GreaterThan`, lies below `Comparison`. The object also inherits `ReductionWithZeroes.isLeftZero` at `TotalComparison`, which answers `false`. That declaration is more specific, so the team's `true` was never reached. The `true` overload is now declared over `TotalComparison`, so it replaces the inherited one: `LessThan` and `GreaterThan` answer `true`, and `EqualTo` `false`. Why: the curator wants the compiled checker's error count on the interpreter's library at zero. This change removed the last of the count's errors in an api file. Other errors kept the count above zero (F-53 holds the count).
56	- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Why: the language has no foreign-function interface, only a planned one, so the library's own practice decides the binding's form. Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. For the runtime's own operations walk's loader answers the helper's name with walk's own operation instead: `ilkName` and `SEQV` (P-167), and the 13 bindings of the arrays' store, threads with `abort` and the task trace (P-169). At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. F-32 counts the bindings that still name a glue class.
57	- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.
58	- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`. So another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. The compiled checker uses coverage only in its overloading rules, to accept an overload set and to justify a call's tie among several most specific declarations, and not in its general subtype test. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, at calls that need no coercion. A ground declaration's types hold no type variable, and `G[\ZZ32\]` is ground. The addendum shows it for coverage used only in that way, and leaves any wider use to a review of its own. A call that needs a coercion is outside the proof too (F-76 gives what the compiled checker does there). A declaration with static parameters, whose instance dispatch must choose at run time, is outside the proof: one instance would have to meet every one of the return types at once. The typing by the intersection is not extended to it, and the specification states that boundary. Rows 543 and 551: the compiled checker gives no call an intersection type where any declaration of the family has static parameters, and walk checks no `comprises` clause declared outside the main component.
59	- P-62 **The `covariant` keyword is future work, off the path to microGPT.** The keyword, with `contravariant`, is the team's 2012 declaration-site variance: under `trait C[\covariant S\]`, a `C[\Dog\]` is a `C[\Animal\]`, as with Scala's `+S`. No library declaration and no line of microGPT uses it. Row 404 records the hole: the compiled checker accepts variance, but the compiled run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`, and walk refuses the program. The future work is declaration-site variance, carried to run time on both paths. When it lands, a rung tries to bring back the specification's sign-refined number types as covariant static parameters. P-80 keeps their design word for word in the specification, marked superseded.
60	- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.
61	- P-147 **An object defines an inherited abstract method when its bodies of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's parameter types.** That is, each value of the abstract method's parameter types is a value of one body's parameter types. A `comprises` clause counts as the compiled checker reads it, which is P-60's reading: a closed trait is covered by its listed types. A body at the abstract method's own parameter types is the plain case. This is the team's rule of 2012, in Steele's abstract-method check of the compiled checker and in the Covered rule of the Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`). So the team's `Library/Pairs.fss` and `ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss` stay valid: an object in each defines an inherited abstract operator once for each type that a `comprises` clause lists. Walk applies the same rule at load, and its earlier allowance of any one narrower body goes. The traits chapter's sentence, which admitted no narrower body, is revised in the specification's revision form (P-96). Row 725: the acceptance of some valid objects whose methods have static parameters of their own, which the checker and walk (row 728) refuse. Row 665: walk's check of generic objects, which its load check skips.
62	- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness in priority: a rung that changes the compiled checker also makes the change fast.** The rung times the checker before and after its change. It first makes the change correct. Then, in the same rung, it makes the new code fast, without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses. So no optimization is left to be done by hand after the landing. Why: the checker must stay usable as it grows. Some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, so that the checker ran past the time limit of the batch gate's count stage, and rungs could not land. The timing is a smoke test: one run of each tree, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. The `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time") gives the steps, their commands and what the rung reports.
63	- P-149 **An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait, and a body for it from a sibling trait, is refused unless it declares the method itself.** In `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives `pick(self)` a body, `O` must declare its own `pick`. Scala's way, where the sibling trait's body implements the abstract method, is not taken. The compiled checker refuses such an object, as the specification's text and the type group's Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`) require. Walk already refuses it at load, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods. A trait that declares one method both abstract and with a body, at the same parameter types, is refused too. Why: the revival honors the designers' intent. It changes Fortress's nature only to reconcile a conflict between the earlier and the later designers' choices, and then looks to other languages for how to do it. Here there is no such conflict, and Fortress is not bent to Scala's way for a hypothetical convenience.
64	- P-151 **Only the `where`-clause forms that the team wrote down are built: conditional extension, a function's or a method's condition, and `AnyList`'s `comprises` clause.** A `where` clause states conditions on static parameters, and may introduce static variables of its own, as `where [\E\]` does. A trait or object that extends a type under a `where` condition is that type only where the condition holds, and its members are checked with the condition holding (conditional extension). A `where` condition on a function's or a method's own static parameters bounds them. The team's commented-out clause `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]` becomes live, which clears the type error of `AnyList`'s join `||`; its other operations, `addLeft` and `addRight`, move into `List` (row 799). `SUM`'s fusion with `MAX` and `MIN`, the library's fast path for the maximum or the minimum of sums, stays. A method's `where` condition clears four of the fusion's six type errors; for the other two, the team's commented-out generic `distribute` is the fix measured (F-242 holds the measurement: as the team wrote it, it only moves them). Why: a feature with little support in the team's work bends the language beyond what the curator can review. He has such a feature built where the team left enough design intent for it, or where it is on the critical path to running fast compiled. Row 773: the members scoped to the condition, since a member checked under it stays callable where the condition fails. Row 774: walk's half of conditional extension. F-181 holds the code generator's half.
65	- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).

<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.
- P-27 **What a program builds that a more mature library would hold goes into the library, in the library's own way.** A program written on this library has a part that states its algorithm, and it can have a part that builds domain-independent machinery that the library lacks, as both microGPT programs do. A form of that second part goes into the standard library when, on reasonable judgment, it is not an extension of the program's own domain; a form that the library has for one number type, rank or sibling trait and lacks for another is the plainest case. Whoever writes it there first studies how the library does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern, such as its `excludes` clauses. This rule governs how the library is extended; it does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language (P-26).
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.

A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.

The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. A program's type declares the coercion inside itself, such as `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits the call with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171): in his words, "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." The team built that coercion under its own names, with the exact value in the numeral ("ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec", commit `128f313b5b`, 2009), but never the four numbers, and no team word calls the names temporary or final; the design keeps what they built, one type for each kind of numeral with its exact value at the coercion, and adds the Draft's names and numbers. The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1, 3 and 6; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`, sections 6 and 7.

- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The class loader, as it makes a generic instance's class, only renames the type parameter, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field; a loader that would, way A4 of array decision A (P-85), is unmeasured (F-18).
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: how the array factory chooses the store of each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an array of a number type, made through the library's generic array traits, gets its unboxed store, `RR64`'s `double[]` first (P-84); B is where unboxed arithmetic happens; and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.
- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Any repair that changes a line of the model is shown to the curator as a diff before it is built. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). - P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar-extension block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** The vocabulary, the array operations that microGPT is written in, declares none of these six operators, an array with a number on either side; the library's scalar-extension block, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, serves them. `Diag`, the vocabulary's diagonal matrix, extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, the method that the library's matrix product calls, so `diag(v) m` scales the rows of `m` without forming the matrix. ### The specification's revision

- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. - P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. ### The suites and the gate

- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.

A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.

It is not tried again unless something significant changes.

It cannot prove a pair over open traits, which no `excludes` or `comprises` clause closes, nor one whose domains exclude only through the exclusion rule and a bound, as the library's `CAP` on `ScalarRange[\I\]` beside `Range2D[\I,J\]` does. It also refuses some pairs that the paper accepts, by its Return Type Rule and by its positional rule, under which two generic declarations in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters by position (F-75). Other gaps have their own owners: two generic arms on a bare type variable fail compiled (F-174, row 537); and walk runs an arm whose size the call leaves unfixed, with the size unbound, where the checker drops the arm or refuses the call (F-69, row 400). Detail: `reviews/overload-static-params-ways.md` sections 2 and 3.
48	- F-51 **A generic call converts a narrower argument for a parameter typed by a type variable that another argument fixes, on both paths.** For `scale[\T\](b: Box[\T\], x: T)` and `b: Box[\RR64\]`, `scale(b, 3)` takes `T = RR64` and converts the `3` (row 388, fixed). So under walk the library's array-scalar `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX`, and the matrix-scalar juxtaposition and `DOT`, take a `ZZ32` scalar with `RR64` elements. F-73 and F-137 give each path's rule. Gated by `tests/InferCoercionRungK` and `compiler_tests/InferCoercionShapes`. Detail: `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review/row388-container-probe.md`.
49	- F-52 **Neither path can use `RationalQuantity` as the specification declares it: the advanced numbers chapter's rational type, refined by `bool` static parameters for its sign, infinities and NaN (`Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`).** The team's `ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss` declares it as the chapter does: a trait that extends its own instantiations with weaker flags, under a `where` clause. The compiled checker refuses it, "Cyclic type hierarchy: Type RationalQuantity transitively extends itself". Walk runs that test only because nothing instantiates the trait; a probe that instantiates it fails under walk. Measured by the note's probes, which `84aef6a4f` removed (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways/Q3*.txt` in its parent). Detail: `reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md`, "Question 3", section 2.
50	- F-53 **At the last landed gate, climb batch 29's, the distance to the switch-over is 0 errors and the checker count is 0.** The distance counts the compiled checker's distinct errors over fourteen components of the interpreter's library and their apis: twelve, and `List`'s two imports, `CovariantCollection` and `OneShotFlag` (F-288). It runs every checker stage of each component whatever the earlier stages reported, and classes the errors by root cause (F-54). At that gate it checks `value object Char` to its end, with no crash (F-334). Row 731's checker gap, which the library's text avoids, stays open for user programs and the team demos (F-285). The checker count checks only the `FortressLibrary` component, with the apis it imports, and each unit stops at its first failing checker stage; the component's run ends clean, which the count stage reads as 0 (`tools/checker-count/run.sh`), and nothing crashes (F-233). A rise in either is reported and turns no gate red on its own; the count stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names, such as a crash that no rung listed (P-39). A rung measured by either takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values: that batch's `compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/gate/distance.txt` and `checker-count.txt`, and the per-site list `compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, which holds the last landed gate's sites, none now (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The checker count and the distance").
